question: Compare the effectiveness of voucher systems and tax incentives in reducing undeclared domestic work across EU Member States, highlighting differences in coverage and equity impacts.
reference: Voucher systems are generally more effective in reducing undeclared domestic work across EU Member States, as they simplify formal employment and make it more affordable, leading to a noticeable decline in informal work. They are broader in coverage and tend to be fairer, though they still face challenges in reaching low-income families. In contrast, tax incentives primarily benefit wealthier households and have a limited impact on reducing undeclared work, with a core criticism being their regressive effect on employing households. Both systems have limitations, but voucher systems are more effective in promoting formal employment and equity.
answer:
Evidence suggests that voucher systems can reduce undeclared domestic work, but their effectiveness varies by country and design. In Belgium, a 2018 study estimated that fewer than 10% of voucher-paid domestic jobs had previously been undeclared, though the scheme’s tax reduction, wage subsidy and administrative simplicity may also have discouraged undeclared work. A separate 2021 study found that Belgian service vouchers halved undeclared work in covered activities. In Sweden, the RUT voucher system is considered probably linked to low undeclared-work levels, but that relationship has not been substantiated; evidence from Austria and Greece indicates low or uncertain impact. Tax incentives also have mixed results: experts reported little effect in Germany, while Spain saw an increase in declared domestic workers after incentives were introduced in 2011, followed by a plateau.

Coverage differs: voucher schemes directly formalise payments for specified domestic services, but may be scarcely used (Austria) or limited by thresholds that reduce their appeal. Tax incentives can apply alongside vouchers or independently, and their impact is also country-specific. Both instruments may help make formal work more attractive, but the pages do not provide a uniform EU-wide comparison of their reach or effectiveness.

Equity concerns are especially clear for tax incentives, which can be regressive because households with higher taxable incomes benefit more. In Germany, households with little or no income-tax liability benefit little or not at all; in Sweden, the highest income decile received 40% of tax deductions. Voucher schemes can also involve unequal distribution of benefits: research on France’s CESU found tax advantages primarily benefited higher-income households, especially the top 10% of earners. Thus, neither approach is uniformly effective or equitable, and impacts depend on national scheme design.

question: Analyze how gender and household status influence underemployment among part-time workers in the EU, and compare the underlying factors driving these patterns.

In contrast, underemployment is more common among young, migrant, single part-time workers and those with lower educational attainment. The reasons for underemployment vary, with difficulties in finding a full-time job being the most common reason, but other factors such as the need to combine paid work with care responsibilities or education also play a role. The probability of underemployment is significantly lower among women, older workers, and people living with partners, and higher among younger workers, migrants, and those with lower educational attainment. These differences cannot be fully explained by occupational and sectoral patterns of employment.

Among part-time workers, women are at least 8 percentage points less likely than men to be underemployed after accounting for other characteristics, and this difference remains when occupational and sectoral employment patterns are considered. Household status also matters: people living with a partner are at least 8 percentage points less likely to be underemployed than singles. But the household effect is much stronger for women: women with small children are 16 percentage points less likely to be underemployed than women without children, and women living with a partner are 9 points less likely than women without a partner. For men, having children or a partner has little effect.

The underlying factors differ. Lower underemployment among women is linked partly to care responsibilities and other unpaid work, which constrain the hours they can consider working; it does not necessarily mean their preferred hours are being met. For partnered workers overall, the document points to household economics: a two-earner household may be able to maintain sufficient income while one person works part-time, whereas single people rely more on their own income and may prefer full-time work. Gendered expectations about men as primary earners and women as primary caregivers also help explain why men in part-time work are more likely to want longer hours.
